title: Score and diffusion methods for inverse data

items.title: Conditional-score and Tweedie identities for Gaussian smoothing

references.title: Giannis Daras et al., A Survey on Diffusion Models for Inverse Problems (2024), arXiv:2410.00083
Yang Song et al., Score-Based Generative Modeling through Stochastic Differential Equations (2021), arXiv:2011.13456
Simon J. D. Prince, Understanding Deep Learning, Chapter 18: Diffusion Models (2026), pp. 363–387; full course notes

items.statement:
Let $d\ge1$, let $\sigma>0$, and let $\mu$ be a probability measure on the Borel subsets of $\mathbb R^d$. Write $\varphi_\sigma(v)=c_{\sigma,d}\exp(-\|v\|^2/(2\sigma^2))$ for the normalized Gaussian density with respect to Lebesgue measure $dx$, define $P_\sigma(du,dx)=\mu(du)\varphi_\sigma(x-u)\,dx$, and set $p_\sigma(x)=\int\varphi_\sigma(x-u)\,\mu(du)$. Define $Q_\sigma(x,du)=\varphi_\sigma(x-u)\mu(du)/p_\sigma(x)$ and $m_\sigma(x)=\int u\,Q_\sigma(x,du)$; under $P_\sigma$, write $X_0(u,x)=u$ and $X_\sigma(u,x)=x$ for the coordinate random vectors, and set $Z=(X_\sigma-X_0)/\sigma$, so $Z\sim N(0,I_d)$ is independent of $X_0$. For Borel maps $h,s:\mathbb R^d	o\mathbb R^d$ that are square-integrable with respect to $p_\sigma(x)dx$, define $R(h)=\int\|h(x)-u\|^2P_\sigma(du,dx)$ and $J(s)=\int\|s(x)-(u-x)/\sigma^2\|^2P_\sigma(du,dx)$. Then $p_\sigma$ is positive and continuously differentiable, $Q_\sigma$ is the conditional law of $X_0$ given $X_\sigma=x$, and $
abla\log p_\sigma(x)=(m_\sigma(x)-x)/\sigma^2$ for every $x\in\mathbb R^d$. If $\int\|u\|^2\,\mu(du)<\infty$, $m_\sigma$ uniquely minimizes $R$ up to $p_\sigma$-almost-everywhere equality. The unique minimizer of $J$ is $
abla\log p_\sigma$, also up to $p_\sigma$-almost-everywhere equality. Under the same Gaussian noising, suppose an observation variable $Y$ is conditionally independent of $Z$ given $X_0$, and, for the fixed observation $y$, $\ell_y:\mathbb R^d	o(0,\infty)$ is the bounded Borel conditional density of $Y$ at $y$ given $X_0=u$, relative to a fixed sigma-finite observation measure, and assume $0<Z_y=\int\ell_y(u)\,\mu(du)<\infty$. Let $\mu_y(du)=\ell_y(u)\mu(du)/Z_y$ and $p_\sigma(x\mid y)=\int\varphi_\sigma(x-u)\,\mu_y(du)$. Then, for $r_\sigma(y\mid x)=\int\ell_y(u)\,Q_\sigma(x,du)$, the conditional score satisfies $
abla_x\log p_\sigma(x\mid y)=
abla_x\log p_\sigma(x)+
abla_x\log r_\sigma(y\mid x)$. No absolute-continuity or bounded-support assumption on $\mu$ is required; $\sigma>0$ supplies the full-support smoothing density.

items.title: Diffusion prior and measurement scores

references.title: Giannis Daras et al., A Survey on Diffusion Models for Inverse Problems (2024), arXiv:2410.00083
Yang Song et al., Score-Based Generative Modeling through Stochastic Differential Equations (2021), arXiv:2011.13456
Hyungjin Chung et al., Diffusion Posterior Sampling for General Noisy Inverse Problems (2023), arXiv:2209.14687

items.statement:
Let $p_\sigma$, $Q_\sigma$, $m_\sigma$, and $r_\sigma(y\mid x)$ be formed under the hypotheses of the conditional-score and Tweedie identities for Gaussian smoothing. The **diffusion prior score** is $s_\sigma(x)=
abla_x\log p_\sigma(x)$, the exact score of the smoothed prior density. The **measurement score** is $g_\sigma(x,y)=
abla_x\log r_\sigma(y\mid x)$, where $r_\sigma(y\mid x)=\int \ell_y(u)\,Q_\sigma(x,du)$ is the likelihood density averaged over the conditional law of the clean state. For general inverse problems, evaluating this clean-state likelihood integral is generally computationally intractable. The **conditional score** is $c_\sigma(x,y)=
abla_x\log p_\sigma(x\mid y)$; it equals $s_\sigma(x)+g_\sigma(x,y)$, and the clean-state conditional mean is $m_\sigma(x)=x+\sigma^2s_\sigma(x)$. A learned field $\widehat s_	heta$ is an estimate of $s_\sigma$ and is exact only when it agrees with $s_\sigma$ almost everywhere under $p_\sigma(x)dx$. Replacing $r_\sigma(y\mid x)$ by the likelihood evaluated at $m_\sigma(x)$ is a plug-in likelihood approximation, not part of the exact measurement-score definition.

items.title: Posterior-mean plug-in measurement scores need not be exact

references.title: Giannis Daras et al., A Survey on Diffusion Models for Inverse Problems (2024), arXiv:2410.00083
Hyungjin Chung et al., Diffusion Posterior Sampling for General Noisy Inverse Problems (2023), arXiv:2209.14687

items.statement: Let $X_0$ take values $-1$ and $1$ with equal probability, let $X_\sigma=X_0+\sigma Z$ with $\sigma>0$ and standard Gaussian noise independent of $X_0$, and let $Y=X_0+\tau W$ for $W\sim N(0,1)$ independent of $(X_0,Z)$, with $\tau>0$. At the observation $y=0$, the exact measurement density $r_\sigma(0\mid x)=\mathbb E[\varphi_\tau(-X_0)\mid X_\sigma=x]$ is constant in $x$, so its score is zero. The exact posterior mean is $m_\sigma(x)=\mathbb E[X_0\mid X_\sigma=x]=\tanh(x/\sigma^2)$, where $\tanh(t)=(e^{2t}-1)/(e^{2t}+1)$. The plug-in density $\varphi_\tau(-m_\sigma(x))$ has score $-m_\sigma(x)m_\sigma'(x)/\tau^2$, which is nonzero for $x\ne0$. Thus evaluating the measurement likelihood at the exact posterior mean does not in general recover the exact measurement score; this example does not rule out equality in special models.

items.title: Weakly convergent finite-step output laws need not be exact

references.title: Giannis Daras et al., A Survey on Diffusion Models for Inverse Problems (2024), arXiv:2410.00083

items.statement: For each integer $m\ge1$, let $\mu_m=(1-2^{-m})\delta_0+2^{-m}\delta_1$ on $\{0,1\}\subset\mathbb R$, where $\delta_a$ is unit mass at $a$, and let the target posterior be $\pi=\delta_0$. For example, this target is the posterior from prior $\delta_0$ and the one-point observation model with likelihood one. The $m$th output law is realized by a one-step instance of the reverse-kernel interface with $N=1$, terminal law $\nu_1=\delta_0$, zero Borel score field, a constant correction into a singleton space, the constant kernel $Q_m(B\mid x,y,a)=\mu_m(B)$, and no projection. Its exact kernel sampler uses at most $m$ independent Bernoulli$(1/2)$ draws and returns $1$ exactly when all draws equal $1$, so it has finite budget for every $m$. The output laws $\mu_m$ converge weakly to $\pi$, yet $\mu_m\ne\pi$ at every finite $m$ because $\mu_m(\{1\})=2^{-m}$. This finite-kernel example illustrates the distinction between asymptotic weak convergence and exact posterior sampling; it is not a performance claim about a trained diffusion model.

items.title: Diffusion inverse solver families and their target laws

references.title: Giannis Daras et al., A Survey on Diffusion Models for Inverse Problems (2024), arXiv:2410.00083
Yang Song et al., Score-Based Generative Modeling through Stochastic Differential Equations (2021), arXiv:2011.13456
Hyungjin Chung et al., Diffusion Posterior Sampling for General Noisy Inverse Problems (2023), arXiv:2209.14687
Simon J. D. Prince, Understanding Deep Learning, Chapter 18: Diffusion Models (2026), pp. 363–387; full course notes

items.statement:
Let $d\ge1$, let $\mu_0$ be a probability measure on $\mathbb R^d$ dominated by a sigma-finite measure $\lambda$, with density $\rho_0=d\mu_0/d\lambda$. Fix an observation vector $y\in\mathbb R^p$ and a nonnegative measurable likelihood function $\ell_y:\mathbb R^d\to[0,\infty)$. Assume $0<Z_y=\int\ell_y(x)\rho_0(x)\,\lambda(dx)<\infty$ and define the posterior probability measure by $\pi_y(dx)=Z_y^{-1}\ell_y(x)\rho_0(x)\,\lambda(dx)$. For the latent-optimization comparison, fix a Borel measurement map $\mathcal A:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^p$. The following diffusion-inverse solver families have different output laws and exactness conditions.

1. **Explicit-score guidance** uses the exact conditional score $c_{\sigma_k}(x,y)=s_{\sigma_k}(x)+g_{\sigma_k}(x,y)$ at each step $t_k$ of a finite schedule $0=t_0<t_1<\dots<t_N$, where a declared map $\sigma:\{t_1,\ldots,t_N\}\to(0,\infty)$ gives $\sigma_k=\sigma(t_k)$ and the forward noising convention is $X_{\sigma_k}=X_0+\sigma_k Z$ with $X_0\sim\mu_0$ and independent $Z\sim N(0,I_d)$. This branch requires the fixed-$y$ likelihood density to be bounded, strictly positive and Borel relative to a fixed sigma-finite observation measure, and the observation variable to be conditionally independent of the Gaussian noising noise given $X_0$, as required by the conditional-score identity. For a finite integer $N\ge1$, let a supplied posterior path probability $\Pi_y$ on $(X_0,\ldots,X_N)$ have $X_0$-marginal $\pi_y$ and terminal marginal $\nu_N$, and let $R_k$ be Borel conditional probability kernels of $X_{k-1}$ given $X_k$ under $\Pi_y$. A reverse-kernel sampler then returns $\pi_y$ when it starts from $\nu_N$, uses each $R_k$ with no projection, and initialization, corrections and transition sampling all succeed almost surely within the declared budgets. If failures are possible, exact kernels alone do not ensure that the law conditional on completed status is the posterior. A learned score, plug-in likelihood, or other surrogate does not supply that certificate by itself.

2. **Variational inference** selects a probability density $q$ with respect to $\lambda$, with $q\ll\pi_y$, and optimizes the evidence lower bound (ELBO) $\operatorname{ELBO}(q)=\int q(x)\log(\ell_y(x)\rho_0(x)/q(x))\,\lambda(dx)$ when the logarithmic integrals are finite, using the convention that the integrand is zero where $q=0$. Its output law is the selected $q$; it equals the posterior only when $q=\pi_y$ as probability measures, equivalently when their densities agree $\lambda$-almost everywhere.

3. **Latent optimization** specifies a latent domain $\mathsf Z$, a generator map $G:\mathsf Z\to\mathbb R^d$, and a deterministic finite-iteration procedure that returns $\widehat z$ using the data-residual objective $\|y-\mathcal A(G(z))\|^2$, without assuming global minimization. Its output law is the point mass $\delta_{G(\widehat z)}$. If $\pi_y$ is not a point mass, this output law is not a posterior draw. A maximum-a-posteriori (MAP) estimate here means a maximizer of the chosen posterior density $Z_y^{-1}\ell_y\rho_0$ with respect to $\lambda$; the measurement-residual objective alone does not establish that claim.

4. **Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC)** uses a probability kernel $K_y$ on the Borel space $\mathbb R^d$, and **sequential Monte Carlo (SMC)** produces a finite weighted particle measure $\widehat\pi_J=\sum_{j=1}^J w_j\delta_{x_j}$ for an integer $J\ge1$, with $w_j\ge0$ and $\sum_jw_j=1$, where $\delta_x$ is unit mass at $x$. If $\pi_y$ is invariant for $K_y$ and a Markov chain starts with law $\pi_y$, every finite-step marginal remains $\pi_y$; invariance alone does not make every initial law exact after finitely many steps. A realized weighted particle measure equals the posterior only when the two measures are equal; every finite empirical measure differs from a non-atomic posterior, meaning one that assigns zero mass to each singleton.

These are law-level distinctions, not performance claims about any trained system.
